title: Check the traceback starting from the last line.
body: A traceback shows the flow of the program from top to bottom where the error occurred. Beginners should first check the error type and message on the last line, and then work their way back up through the file and line numbers.
detail: The last line usually displays the error type—such as `ValueError` or `TypeError`—along with a human-readable message. Then, by following the `File` and `line` information at the top, you can narrow down where the problem originated—in which file and on which line. It’s best to read the error message first, and then work backward to check the input values or variable states that caused it.

title: "File" and "line" are clues for finding the location to correct.
body: The "File" and "line" fields in a traceback indicate the location in the code where the error occurred. By looking at the filename and line number together, you can quickly identify potential areas to fix and verify what values were passed.
detail: When multiple functions call one another, the traceback may list the file and line number multiple times. In this case, it’s safest to first check the line of your code closest to the bottom and then work your way back up to determine which value was incorrect on that line. If you only see lines from within a library, you’ll need to locate the line in your code that called that library as well.

title: `raise` intentionally raises an error
body: `raise` is a syntax that directly throws an exception when it detects problematic input or a problematic state. Instead of silently proceeding, it halts the execution flow and reveals the cause, leaving a clue for debugging.
detail: For example, if a score is negative, it may be safer to raise a `ValueError` to indicate that the input is invalid rather than continuing with the calculation. `raise` is not a syntax that annoys users; it is a mechanism that prevents the code from proceeding in an incorrect state. If you include a description of which condition was violated in the message, you can identify the cause more quickly when reading the traceback later.

title: "Finally" is often used in cleanup tasks.
body: The `finally` block is executed at the end, regardless of whether an error occurs or not. It is often used for cleanup tasks that must be completed—such as closing files, releasing locks, and cleaning up temporary state—and it executes even in the event of a failure.
detail: Even if you perform an operation in the `try` block and handle errors in the `except` block, there may still be cleanup code that must be executed at the end. The `finally` block serves to group that code in one place. However, for complex file operations, the `with` statement is often more readable. Beginners should simply remember that `finally` is for "cleanup at the end, regardless of success or failure."

title: The "except" clause should be as specific as possible.
body: If you use `except` too broadly, it can obscure the nature of the problem. Whenever possible, you should catch specific types of exceptions—such as `ValueError`—to make it easier to distinguish between actual bugs and expected failures.
detail: If you catch all exceptions using `except:`, you might quietly overlook typos, incorrect variables, and even unexpected bugs. As a beginner, you should get into the habit of reading the specific `except` clause first to distinguish between a failure you anticipated and a bug that needs to be fixed. For example, if it’s a numeric conversion failure, it’s better for debugging to catch it with a more specific exception like `ValueError`.

title: If you silently suppress errors, debugging becomes more difficult.
body: If you do nothing inside the `except` block or return a meaningless value, you may miss the actual cause. You need to log the reason for the failure or reproduce it so that you can track down the same problem later.
detail: Beginners often assume a problem is solved simply because the error is no longer displayed on the screen. However, if you move on without documenting the cause, it becomes difficult to trace the issue later when data is missing or results appear abnormal. You need to consider logging, error messages, and strategies for handling recurrence together. In particular, if you only use `pass` inside an `except` block or return meaningless default values, actual bugs can be quietly hidden.
